title: Roots, Rational Powers, and Classical Inequalities: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Rational powers of rational bases computed from the definition
items.statement: In $\mathbb{R}$, with the rational powers of [[def-rational-power]]: $(4/9)^{1/2} = 2/3$; $(8/27)^{1/3} = 2/3$; $(4/9)^{3/2} = 8/27$; $(27/8)^{-2/3} = 4/9$; and $8^{2/6} = 8^{1/3} = 2$, one value produced from either representative of the rational $1/3 = 2/6$. Every base occurring is a positive rational and every exponent a rational with numerator an integer and denominator a natural $\ge 1$, so the definition applies in each case; the last display is the instance of [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] that [[def-rational-power]] records in its `justified_by`. The item also checks the negative-exponent and non-coprime-representative cases, the two places where the definition is most easily misread.
items.strategy: (i) $2/3$ is the nonnegative square root of $4/9$ and the nonnegative cube root of $8/27$, since $(2/3)^{2} = 4/9$ and $(2/3)^{3} = 8/27$ by field arithmetic; uniqueness in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] therefore gives $(4/9)^{1/2} = 2/3$ and $(8/27)^{1/3} = 2/3$, using the representatives $1/2$ and $1/3$, whose denominators are $2$ and $3$ respectively. (ii) At the representative $3/2$ the definition gives $(4/9)^{3/2} = \big((4/9)^{1/2}\big)^{3} = (2/3)^{3} = 8/27$. (iii) At the representative $-2/3$ it gives $(27/8)^{-2/3} = \big((27/8)^{1/3}\big)^{-2} = (3/2)^{-2} = \big((3/2)^{2}\big)^{-1} = (9/4)^{-1} = 4/9$, the negative exponent being the clause of [[def-integer-power]] and the last step the uniqueness of inverses. (iv) $8^{1/3} = 2$ because $2^{3} = 8$ and $2 \ge 0$; since $2/6 = 1/3$ in $\mathbb{Q}$, [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] gives $8^{2/6} = 8^{1/3}$. Every step stays inside the hypotheses of [[def-rational-power]]; no value is assigned to a negative base.

items.title: Odd powers are bijections of $\mathbb{R}$: $x^{3} = -8$ has the unique solution $x = -2$
items.statement: Let $n \ge 1$ be odd. Then $x \mapsto x^{n}$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}$ onto $\mathbb{R}$: every real number has exactly one real $n$-th root. Explicitly, $x^{3} = -8$ has the unique solution $x = -2$, and $x^{5} = -32$ has the unique solution $x = -2$. For a negative right-hand side this is a statement about the solution of $x^{n} = a$; it does not extend the symbol $a^{1/n}$, since [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] produces that symbol only for $a \ge 0$ and [[def-rational-power]] does not define rational powers of negative bases (its separate zero-base clause concerns nonnegative bases only). This is the claim the A-page prose records when it says that odd roots of negatives do exist while [[fs-negative-has-square-root]] shows that even ones do not.
items.strategy: Existence: let $a \in \mathbb{R}$. If $a \ge 0$, take $y := a^{1/n}$ from [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]. If $a < 0$, put $b := -a > 0$ and $y := b^{1/n} \ge 0$, and set $x := -y$; then $x^{n} = (-y)^{n} = (-1)^{n}y^{n} = -y^{n} = -b = a$, where $(-y)^{n} = (-1)^{n}y^{n}$ is the product law of [[lem-power-laws]], $(-1)^{n} = -1$ for odd $n$ is an induction from that same law, and $(-1)(-1) = 1$ is [[lem-of-mult-neg]]. Injectivity: suppose $x \ne y$. If $0 \le x < y$ then $x^{n} < y^{n}$ by [[lem-power-monotone]]. If $x < y \le 0$ then $0 \le -y < -x$, so $(-y)^{n} < (-x)^{n}$ by monotonicity, that is $-y^{n} < -x^{n}$ by the odd-power identity, equivalently $x^{n} < y^{n}$ by the sign rules of [[lem-of-sign-rules]]. If $x < 0 \le y$ then $x^{n} < 0 \le y^{n}$ by the odd-power identity and $u^{n} > 0$ for $u > 0$. So $x \mapsto x^{n}$ is injective, hence bijective by the existence argument. The displayed solutions follow from $(-2)^{3} = -8$ and $(-2)^{5} = -32$ by [[def-integer-power]], uniqueness being the injectivity proved. No continuity and no completeness beyond [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] is used, so the argument is choice-free.

items.title: The two-term AM-GM inequality, its equality case, and $x + x^{-1} \ge 2$
items.statement: (a) For all $a, b \ge 0$, $\dfrac{a+b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}$, equivalently $ab \le \Big(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\Big)^{2}$, with equality in either form exactly when $a = b$. (b) Consequently, for every $x > 0$, $x + x^{-1} \ge 2$, with equality exactly when $x = 1$.
items.strategy: (a) is [[thm-am-gm]] at $n = 2$ with $a_0 := a$, $a_1 := b$: the geometric mean is $(ab)^{1/2}$, which is $\sqrt{ab}$ by [[def-rational-power]] and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]; the equality clause is the theorem's; and the equivalence of the two displays is the strict monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives, that is $ab \le A^{2} \iff (ab)^{1/2} \le A$ for $A \ge 0$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]). (b) Apply (a) to $a_0 := x$ and $a_1 := x^{-1}$ (the negative integer power of [[def-integer-power]]): the product is $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$, so the geometric mean is $1^{1/2} = 1$ by [[lem-rational-power-laws]], and the arithmetic mean is $(x + x^{-1})/2$. Equality in (a) means $x = x^{-1}$, equivalently $x^{2} = 1$; for $x > 0$ this holds exactly at $x = 1$, since $0 < x < 1$ gives $x^{2} < 1^{2} = 1$ and $x > 1$ gives $x^{2} > 1^{2} = 1$ by [[lem-power-monotone]].

items.title: Comparing rational powers: $2^{1/3} < 2^{1/2} < 3^{1/3}$
items.statement: (i) $2^{1/2} > 2^{1/3}$; (ii) $3^{1/2} > 2^{1/2}$; (iii) $2^{1/2} < 3^{1/3}$; hence $2^{1/3} < 2^{1/2} < 3^{1/3}$. All bases are positive and all exponents rational, so [[def-rational-power]] applies. Clauses (i) and (ii) are instances of the two monotonicity statements of [[lem-rational-power-monotone]], but (iii) is not: it compares bases $2 < 3$ against exponents in the opposite order $1/2 > 1/3$, and neither monotonicity clause decides it.
items.strategy: (i) $2 > 1$ and $1/3 < 1/2$, so exponent monotonicity gives $2^{1/3} < 2^{1/2}$. (ii) $1/2 > 0$ and $2 < 3$, so base monotonicity gives $2^{1/2} < 3^{1/2}$. (iii) Raise both sides of the desired comparison to the sixth power: $\big(2^{1/2}\big)^{6} = 2^{(1/2)\cdot 6} = 2^{3} = 8$ and $\big(3^{1/3}\big)^{6} = 3^{(1/3)\cdot 6} = 3^{2} = 9$ by the iterated-power law of [[lem-rational-power-laws]] together with [[def-integer-power]]; since $8 < 9$, the strict monotonicity of $t \mapsto t^{6}$ on $[0,\infty)$ ([[lem-power-monotone]], using $2^{1/2} \ge 0$ and $3^{1/3} \ge 0$ from [[def-rational-power]]) gives $2^{1/2} < 3^{1/3}$. Chaining (i) and (iii) gives the displayed order. The route in (iii) is the standard one for comparisons that no single monotonicity clause reaches.

items.title: A weighted AM-GM computation: $8^{2/3}\,1^{1/3} \le \frac{2}{3}\cdot 8 + \frac{1}{3}\cdot 1$
items.statement: Take $n := 2$, $x_0 := 8$, $x_1 := 1$ and the rational weights $w_0 := 2/3$, $w_1 := 1/3$, so that $\iota(w_0) + \iota(w_1) = 1$ in $\mathbb{R}$. Then [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] gives $$8^{2/3}\cdot 1^{1/3} \;\le\; \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot 8 + \tfrac{1}{3}\cdot 1,$$ where the left-hand side is $4$ and the right-hand side is $17/3$; so $4 < 17/3$ and the inequality is strict here. With $x_0 := x_1 := 8$ instead, both sides equal $8$, so the bound is attained by a constant list.
items.strategy: $8^{1/3} = 2$ since $2^{3} = 8$ and $2 \ge 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]), so $8^{2/3} = \big(8^{1/3}\big)^{2} = 4$ by the definition at the representative $2/3$; and $1^{1/3} = 1$ since $1^{3} = 1$. The right-hand side is $(2/3)\cdot 8 + (1/3)\cdot 1 = 16/3 + 1/3 = 17/3$ by the scaling and addition laws of finite sums ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $4 = 12/3 < 17/3$. For the constant list $x_0 = x_1 = 8$, the addition law of [[lem-rational-power-laws]] gives $8^{2/3}\,8^{1/3} = 8^{2/3 + 1/3} = 8^{1} = 8$, which equals $(2/3)\cdot 8 + (1/3)\cdot 8$ by scaling. No equality characterization of weighted AM-GM is claimed — [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] records the inequality only — which is why the second display is verified by direct computation.

items.title: Young's inequality at $p = q = 2$ and at $p = 3$, $q = 3/2$
items.statement: (i) At the conjugate pair $p = q = 2$, [[thm-young-inequality]] reads $ab \le \frac{a^{2}}{2} + \frac{b^{2}}{2}$ for all $a, b \ge 0$, with equality exactly when $a = b$; the instance $a := 4$, $b := 9$ gives $36 \le 97/2$. (ii) At $p := 3$ and $q := 3/2$, conjugate since $\frac13 + \frac23 = 1$, it reads $ab \le \frac{a^{3}}{3} + \frac{2}{3}\,b^{3/2}$; the instance $a := 2$, $b := 4$ gives $8$ on both sides.
items.strategy: (i) The inequality is [[thm-young-inequality]] at $p = q = 2$. For the equality clause, apply [[thm-am-gm]] at $n = 2$ to the nonnegative list $(a^{2}, b^{2})$ — exactly the weighted-AM-GM step of [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] at the weights $1/2, 1/2$. Its geometric mean is $(a^{2}b^{2})^{1/2} = ab$, since $ab \ge 0$ and $(ab)^{2} = a^{2}b^{2}$ by [[lem-power-laws]] make $ab$ the nonnegative square root of $a^{2}b^{2}$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]); and its equality clause says that equality holds exactly when $a^{2} = b^{2}$, which for $a, b \ge 0$ means $a = b$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]). The instance is arithmetic: $(4^{2} + 9^{2})/2 = 97/2 \ge 36 = 4\cdot 9$. (ii) $1/3 + 2/3 = 1$ by rational arithmetic, so the theorem applies; the instance evaluates $a^{3}/3 = 8/3$ and $(2/3)\,b^{3/2} = (2/3)\big(4^{1/2}\big)^{3} = (2/3)\cdot 8 = 16/3$, whose sum is $8 = ab$.

items.title: The two-term Lagrange identity and Cauchy-Schwarz
items.statement: For all reals $a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1$, $$(a_0^{2} + a_1^{2})(b_0^{2} + b_1^{2}) - (a_0b_0 + a_1b_1)^{2} = (a_0b_1 - a_1b_0)^{2};$$ consequently $(a_0b_0 + a_1b_1)^{2} \le (a_0^{2} + a_1^{2})(b_0^{2} + b_1^{2})$, with equality exactly when $a_0b_1 = a_1b_0$ — the two-entry form of the proportionality clause of [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]]. The instance $a_0 := 1$, $a_1 := 2$, $b_0 := 3$, $b_1 := 4$ reads $5\cdot 25 - 121 = 4 = (-2)^{2}$.
items.strategy: Expand the left-hand difference with distributivity over the two-entry sums ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]): $a_0^{2}b_0^{2} + a_0^{2}b_1^{2} + a_1^{2}b_0^{2} + a_1^{2}b_1^{2} - \big(a_0^{2}b_0^{2} + 2a_0b_0a_1b_1 + a_1^{2}b_1^{2}\big)$ cancels to $a_0^{2}b_1^{2} - 2(a_0b_1)(a_1b_0) + a_1^{2}b_0^{2} = (a_0b_1 - a_1b_0)^{2}$, using $(-c)^{2} = c^{2}$ and $(-1)^{2} = 1$ from [[lem-power-laws]] and [[lem-of-mult-neg]]. The difference is a square: if its base is zero then the square is $0$ by [[def-integer-power]], while a nonzero base has a positive square by [[lem-of-square-positive]]. Thus the difference is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when $a_0b_1 - a_1b_0 = 0$; rearranging gives the inequality and its equality case. The instance is a direct evaluation. This derivation uses no root and reproduces, in the two-entry case, the expansion route by which [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]] is proved; the root form of that theorem needs [[thm-of-square-roots]] and is not used here.

items.title: Hölder at the conjugate pair $p = 3$, $q = 3/2$: an exact equality instance and a strict instance
items.statement: $p := 3$ and $q := 3/2$ are conjugate rationals, $\frac13 + \frac23 = 1$. For the two-entry lists $a_0 = a_1 = b_0 = b_1 = 1$, [[thm-holder-finite]] reads $$\sum_{k<2}|a_kb_k| = 2 \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<2}|a_k|^{3}\Big)^{1/3}\Big(\sum_{k<2}|b_k|^{3/2}\Big)^{2/3} = 2^{1/3}\,2^{2/3} = 2,$$ so both sides are equal here. For $a = (2,0)$ and $b = (0,3)$ the inequality is strict: the left-hand side is $0$ and the right-hand side is $2\cdot 3 = 6$.
items.strategy: Compute the finite sums at $k = 0, 1$ from [[def-finite-sum]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]; $1^{r} = 1$ for each positive rational $r$; and $2^{1/3}\,2^{2/3} = 2^{1/3 + 2/3} = 2^{1} = 2$ by the addition law of [[lem-rational-power-laws]]. In the strict instance, $(8)^{1/3} = 2$ and $\big(3^{3/2}\big)^{2/3} = 3^{(3/2)(2/3)} = 3^{1} = 3$ by the iterated-power law, with $0 < 6$. Only the inequality is claimed: [[thm-holder-finite]] records no equality characterization, and none is asserted here.

items.title: Minkowski for two-entry vectors: equality and strict cases
items.statement: For all reals $x_0, x_1, y_0, y_1$, $$\big((x_0+y_0)^{2} + (x_1+y_1)^{2}\big)^{1/2} \;\le\; \big(x_0^{2} + x_1^{2}\big)^{1/2} + \big(y_0^{2} + y_1^{2}\big)^{1/2},$$ and equality holds exactly when $x_0y_1 = x_1y_0$ and $x_0y_0 + x_1y_1 \ge 0$. Two instances: for $x = (3,4)$ and $y = (6,8)$ both sides are $15$; for $x = (3,4)$ and $y = (4,-3)$ the left-hand side is $\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$ and the right-hand side is $10$, so the inequality is strict.
items.strategy: The inequality is [[thm-minkowski-finite]] at $p = 2$, with $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-abs-value]]). Equality analysis: write $A := x_0^{2}+x_1^{2}$, $B := y_0^{2}+y_1^{2}$ and $C := x_0y_0 + x_1y_1$; expanding gives $A + 2C + B$ for the squared left side and $A + B + 2\sqrt{A}\sqrt{B} = A + B + 2\sqrt{AB}$ for the squared right side, the last step by the product law of [[lem-rational-power-laws]]. Both sides are nonnegative, so equality holds exactly when the squares agree ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]), that is exactly when $C = \sqrt{AB}$; and $C = \sqrt{AB}$ holds exactly when $C \ge 0$ and $C^{2} = AB$. The exact identity and equality clause of the already derived [[ex-cauchy-schwarz-lagrange-identity-two-terms]] give $AB-C^{2}=(x_0y_1-x_1y_0)^{2}\ge0$, with equality exactly when $x_0y_1=x_1y_0$. This is the stated condition and handles zero vectors as well as nonzero vectors. The two instances are direct computations: for $x = (3,4)$ and $y = (6,8)$, $x+y = (9,12)$ has $9^{2}+12^{2} = 225 = 15^{2}$ while $5 + 10 = 15$; for $x = (3,4)$ and $y = (4,-3)$, $x+y = (7,1)$ has squared length $50$, so the left side is $\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25}\,\sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2}$ by the product law, and $5\sqrt{2} < 10$ because $0 \le \sqrt{2} < 2$ (from $2 < 4 = 2^{2}$ by [[lem-of-square-monotone]]) and $5 > 0$. Here $x_0y_1 - x_1y_0 = 3(-3) - 4\cdot 4 = -25 \ne 0$, consistent with the equality criterion.

items.title: AM-GM fails for negative entries: $(-1,-4)$ has geometric mean $2$ and arithmetic mean $-5/2$
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** the conclusion $\sqrt{ab} \le \dfrac{a+b}{2}$ of the two-term arithmetic-geometric mean inequality holds for arbitrary real $a, b$. Witness: $a := -1$, $b := -4$. The product is $ab = 4$, so the geometric mean is $4^{1/2} = 2$, while the arithmetic mean is $(-1-4)/2 = -5/2$; thus $G = 2 > -5/2 = A$ and the inequality fails. The failure is not an accident of the witness: for any two negative entries $a, b < 0$ the product is positive, so $G > 0$, while $A < 0$, giving $G > A$. A second failure mode is non-existence: for $a := -1$, $b := 1$ the product is $-1$, which has no real square root ([[fs-negative-has-square-root]]), so $G$ is not defined at all. By contrast the equivalent squared form $ab \le A^{2}$ of [[thm-am-gm]] survives for all real $a, b$, since $A^{2} - ab = (a-b)^{2}/4 \ge 0$; the hypothesis $a, b \ge 0$ is spent exactly on passing from that squared form to the geometric-mean form, which needs a nonnegative arithmetic mean and a real geometric mean.
items.strategy: Evaluate $ab = 4$ and $A = -5/2$ by field arithmetic, and $G = 4^{1/2} = 2$ from [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] since $2 \ge 0$ and $2^{2} = 4$; then $2 > -5/2$ because $-5/2 < 0 < 2$ by [[cor-of-one-positive]] and [[lem-of-sign-rules]]. For the general negative-pair statement, $a, b < 0$ give $ab > 0$ ([[lem-of-sign-rules]]), so $G = (ab)^{1/2} > 0$, while $A = (a+b)/2 < 0$; the comparison follows from trichotomy. The non-existence clause is [[fs-negative-has-square-root]]. For the closing observation, $4A^{2} - 4ab = (a+b)^{2} - 4ab = (a-b)^{2} \ge 0$ by [[lem-of-square-positive]], so $ab \le A^{2}$; this displays precisely what the nonnegativity hypothesis is needed for, namely that $A$ is itself a mean of nonnegative entries and $(ab)^{1/2}$ a real number. For the square argument, a zero difference gives square $0$ by field multiplication, while a nonzero difference has positive square by the actual hypothesis of [[lem-of-square-positive]]; this verifies nonnegativity including equality rather than misapplying its strict clause at zero.

items.title: Weighted AM-GM needs nonnegative weights summing to $1$
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** the inequality $\prod_{k<n} x_k^{w_k} \le \sum_{k<n} w_k x_k$ of [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] holds for all positive $x_k$ and all rational weights $w_k$ of sum $1$, or for all rational weights whatsoever. Two witnesses. (i) For $x_0 := x_1 := 4$ and $w_0 := w_1 := 1$, whose sum is $2 \ne 1$: the left-hand side is $4^{1}\cdot 4^{1} = 16$ and the right-hand side is $1\cdot 4 + 1\cdot 4 = 8$, so $16 > 8$. (ii) For $x_0 := 4$, $x_1 := 1/4$, $w_0 := 2$ and $w_1 := -1$, whose sum is $1$ but which contains a negative weight: the left-hand side is $4^{2}\cdot(1/4)^{-1} = 16\cdot 4 = 64$ and the right-hand side is $2\cdot 4 + (-1)\cdot(1/4) = 8 - 1/4 = 31/4$, so $64 > 31/4$. Both hypotheses on the weights — nonnegativity and total mass $1$ — are therefore load-bearing.
items.strategy: Verify each power by [[def-rational-power]] and [[lem-rational-power-laws]]: $4^{1} = 4$; $(1/4)^{-1} = \big((1/4)^{1}\big)^{-1} = 4$ via the negative-exponent clause of [[def-integer-power]]; and the sums are field computations in $\mathbb{R}$ with the weights read through the embedding $\iota$ of [[lem-of-q-embeds]]. The comparisons $16 > 8$ and $64 > 31/4$ follow from [[cor-of-one-positive]] and the order rules ($64 = 256/4 > 31/4$). In (ii) the weight $-1$ is a legitimate rational by [[def-rationals]]; the point is that [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] requires $w_k \ge 0$, and the example shows the conclusion fails without it even when $\sum_k \iota(w_k) = 1$.

items.title: Minkowski fails for $p = 1/2$: the hypothesis $p \ge 1$ is load-bearing
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** the inequality of [[thm-minkowski-finite]] holds for every positive rational $p$. Witness: $p := 1/2$, with the two-entry lists $x_0 := 1$, $x_1 := 0$ and $y_0 := 0$, $y_1 := 1$. The left-hand side $\big(\sum_{k<2}|x_k+y_k|^{1/2}\big)^{1/(1/2)} = \big(\sum_{k<2}|x_k+y_k|^{1/2}\big)^{2}$ is $(1+1)^{2} = 4$, while the right-hand side $\big(\sum_{k<2}|x_k|^{1/2}\big)^{2} + \big(\sum_{k<2}|y_k|^{1/2}\big)^{2}$ is $1 + 1 = 2$; so the inequality fails. Every expression is defined: $1/2$ is a positive rational, $|z|^{1/2} = \sqrt{|z|}$ is the rational power of [[def-rational-power]] with its supplementary clause $0^{1/2} = 0$, and the outer exponent $1/p = 2$ is an integer power.
items.strategy: Compute: $|1|^{1/2} = 1^{1/2} = 1$ since $1 \ge 0$ and $1^{2} = 1$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]], [[def-rational-power]]); $|0|^{1/2} = 0$ by the supplementary clause; the two-term sums are $1 + 1 = 2$ by [[def-finite-sum]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]; the outer squares are [[def-integer-power]]. Then $4 > 2$ by [[cor-of-one-positive]] and the order rules, since $4 = 2 + 2 > 2$. The example shows that the conclusion of [[thm-minkowski-finite]] is genuinely false outside its hypothesis $p \ge 1$ and cannot be read as an artefact of undefined powers.

references.locator: Chapter 13 §13.7, Theorem 13.96 and its standing hypothesis 1 < p < ∞, printed pp. 298-299

items.title: Bernoulli fails for $x < -1$: $x = -4$, $n = 3$
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** $(1+x)^{n} \ge 1 + nx$ holds for every real $x$ and every natural $n$. Witness: $x := -4$, $n := 3$. Then $(1+x)^{3} = (-3)^{3} = -27$ while $1 + 3x = -11$, so $(1+x)^{3} < 1 + 3x$ and the inequality fails. Two boundary remarks sharpen the failure: at $n = 1$ the two sides agree for every $x$, so the failure needs $n \ge 2$; and at $x = -3$, $n = 3$ the two sides happen to agree ($-8 = -8$), so a witness must be chosen rather than assumed. The hypothesis $x \ge -1$ of [[lem-bernoulli-inequality]] is therefore load-bearing.
items.strategy: Evaluate $(1+x)^{3} = (-3)^{3} = -27$ and $1 + 3x = -11$ by [[def-integer-power]] and field arithmetic; the comparison $-27 < -11$ is equivalent to $0 < 16$, which is [[cor-of-one-positive]] and the order rules of [[lem-of-sign-rules]] and [[lem-of-add-order]]. The two boundary remarks are direct evaluations: $(1+x)^{1} = 1 + x = 1 + 1\cdot x$ by the recursion clause; and $(1-3)^{3} = (-2)^{3} = -8 = 1 + 3(-3)$.

items.title: The iterated rational-power law fails without a positive base: $\big((-3)^{2}\big)^{1/2} = 3 \ne -3$
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** the identity $(a^{r})^{s} = a^{rs}$ of [[lem-rational-power-laws]] holds for every real $a$ and all rationals $r, s$ for which both sides are defined. Witness: $a := -3$, $r := 2$, $s := 1/2$. Here $a^{r}$ is the integer power $(-3)^{2} = 9$, so $(a^{r})^{s} = 9^{1/2} = 3$ by [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], while $a^{rs} = (-3)^{1} = -3$ is again an integer power; the two sides differ. Both displayed expressions are defined by the library's definitions — only the rational-power step, on the positive base $9$, uses [[def-rational-power]] — so the positivity hypothesis $a > 0$ in [[lem-rational-power-laws]] cannot be dropped. The correct general statement in this case is that $\big(a^{2}\big)^{1/2} = |a|$ for every real $a$.
items.strategy: $(-3)^{2} = 9$ and $(-3)^{1} = -3$ are [[def-integer-power]] evaluations; $9^{1/2} = 3$ since $3 \ge 0$ and $3^{2} = 9$, by uniqueness in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]. The two values differ because $3 \ne -3$. For the closing statement: $a^{2} \ge 0$ so $\big(a^{2}\big)^{1/2}$ exists, and $|a| \ge 0$ with $|a|^{2} = a^{2}$ by [[lem-of-abs-value]]; uniqueness of the nonnegative square root therefore gives $\big(a^{2}\big)^{1/2} = |a|$, which is precisely the failure of $(a^{r})^{s} = a^{rs}$ when $a < 0$: the left side is $|a|$, not $a$. No integer-power law is being denied — [[lem-power-laws]] permits zero bases for its natural-exponent identities and requires nonzero bases for its extension to all integer exponents — and the counterexample isolates the rational-power hypothesis.

items.title: Five finite proofs of Bernoulli, with rational exponents and the quadratic refinement
items.statement: Five proof routes verify the same integer statement: for $x\ge-1$ and a natural $n$, $(1+x)^n\ge1+nx$, with equality exactly when $n\le1$ or $x=0$. The routes are ordinary induction, geometric-sum comparison, an exact nonnegative supporting-line remainder, AM-GM, and a finite binomial/positive-weight expansion. They cover $-1\le x<0$ as well as $x\ge0$; $0^0=1$ is the integer-power convention. In addition, with rational $r$ and $x\ge-1$ (requiring $x>-1$ when $r<0$), $(1+x)^r\ge1+rx$ for $r\ge1$ or $r\le0$, and $(1+x)^r\le1+rx$ for $0\le r\le1$. Equality is exactly $x=0$ or $r\in\{0,1\}$. For rational $r\ge2$, the promised quadratic refinement follows in the stronger form $(1+x)^r\ge1+rx+(r/2)x^2$; hence it holds with any natural coefficient $m$ satisfying $2m\le r$, including the coefficient customarily written $\lfloor r/2\rfloor$. For $1\le r<2$ that floor coefficient is zero and the ordinary bound applies. The stronger refinement has equality exactly when $x=0$ or $r=2$. At $x=-1$, the supplementary clause of [[def-rational-power]] supplies $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$, and [[def-integer-power]] supplies $0^0=1$; negative powers of zero remain undefined. No irrational exponent or exponential/general convexity theorem is asserted.
items.strategy:
Write $y=1+x\ge0$, and use the canonical natural/rational embeddings in every real-field formula. Finite sums below are sums in $\mathbb R$, and all powers in the first five routes have natural exponents. Separate $n=0,1$ and $x=0$ first: these give equality immediately. The remaining case is $n\ge2$, $y\ge0$, $y\ne1$.

Route 1, ordinary induction: use the proved induction argument and equality clause of [[lem-bernoulli-inequality]], not a newly minted duplicate supplier. Its step is $y^{n+1}\ge(1+nx)y=1+(n+1)x+nx^2$, since $y\ge0$ licenses multiplication and $nx^2\ge0$. To see strictness without losing the $y=0$ endpoint, start from $y^2-(1+2x)=x^2>0$. If $y>0$, multiply the strict inequality at $n$ by $y$ and discard $nx^2\ge0$; if $y=0$, the right side $1-n$ is strictly negative for $n\ge2$.

Route 2, geometric-sum comparison: [[lem-power-difference-factorisation]] at bases $1,y$ gives $y^n-1=(y-1)\sum_{k<n}y^k$. If $y>1$, every term is at least $1$ and the $k=1$ term is strictly greater for $n\ge2$, so the sum is $>n$ and multiplication by $y-1>0$ gives the strict Bernoulli bound. If $0\le y<1$, every term is at most $1$ and the $k=1$ term is strictly smaller, including $y=0$; thus the sum is $<n$, and multiplication by the negative $y-1$ reverses the inequality. This proves the full negative-$x$ range, not just the positive range.

Route 3, exact supporting-line remainder: for $n\ge2$, finite distributivity and telescoping give $y^n-1-n(y-1)=(y-1)^2\sum_{j=0}^{n-2}(n-1-j)y^j$. Derive the identity locally: multiplying the last sum by $y-1$ cancels adjacent coefficients and gives $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}y^k-(n-1)$; multiplying once more gives $y^n-ny+(n-1)$. Each term in the original sum is nonnegative for $y\ge0$ and its constant term is the positive real image of $n-1$. Hence the remainder is positive unless $y=1$. This supplies the power function's supporting line at $1$ directly, without an unproved convexity lemma.

Route 4, AM-GM: apply the existing [[thm-am-gm]] to the $n$ nonnegative entries $y^n,1,\ldots,1$. Their product is $y^n$ and its unique nonnegative $n$th root is $y$. Thus $ny\le y^n+n-1$, precisely Bernoulli. For $n\ge2$, equality forces $y^n=1$ by the theorem's equality clause, and then $y=1$ by [[lem-power-monotone]]. At $y=0$, the theorem still applies to nonnegative entries.

Route 5, finite binomial expansion on both signs: construct real coefficients $b_{0,0}=1$, $b_{0,k}=0$ outside $k=0$, and $b_{n+1,k}=b_{n,k}+b_{n,k-1}$, extending each finite row by zero outside $0\le k\le n$. The existence of successive finite rows is recursion; no combinatorial counting theorem is assumed. Induction gives $b_{n,0}=b_{n,n}=1$, $b_{n,1}=n$, and $b_{n,k}\ge0$, as well as $(u+v)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}b_{n,k}u^kv^{n-k}$: multiply the preceding finite expansion by $u+v$, shift the index in one sum and use the row recursion. It also gives $k b_{n,k}=n b_{n-1,k-1}$ for $1\le k\le n$: apply the preceding-row identities to $k(b_{n-1,k}+b_{n-1,k-1})$, rewrite the second part as $(k-1)b_{n-1,k-1}+b_{n-1,k-1}$, and combine with the Pascal recursion to obtain $n b_{n-1,k-1}$; handle $k=1,n$ by the endpoint identities. These are identities in the real field after embedding the natural indices. For $x>0$, use $(u,v)=(x,1)$; subtracting the $k=0,1$ terms leaves only nonnegative terms and the $k=n$ term $x^n>0$. For $-1\le x<0$, put $t=-x\in(0,1]$, $y=1-t\ge0$. The same expansion and the coefficient identity give $1=(t+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}b_{n,k}t^ky^{n-k}$ and $nt=\sum_{k=1}^{n} k b_{n,k}t^ky^{n-k}$. Subtracting yields $nt-(1-y^n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(k-1)b_{n,k}t^ky^{n-k}\ge0$, strictly so from the $k=n$ term $(n-1)t^n>0$. Thus $y^n>1-nt=1+nx$. This proves the negative range by positive weights, not by illegally dropping alternating-sign terms in the expansion of $(1+x)^n$.

Rational extension: now require $y=1+x>0$. Apply the existing two-term [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] only with positive bases and nonnegative rational weights summing to one. For $r>1$, bases $y^r,1$ and weights $1/r,1-1/r$ give $y\le y^r/r+1-1/r$. For $r<0$, bases $y,y^r$ and weights $-r/(1-r),1/(1-r)$ have geometric product $1$ by [[lem-rational-power-laws]], so $1\le(-ry+y^r)/(1-r)$. For $0<r<1$, bases $y,1$ and weights $r,1-r$ give $y^r\le ry+1-r$. Rearrange each inequality by multiplying positive denominators. Handle $r=0,1$ separately. The weighted supplier does not state an equality clause, so prove the needed strictness: write the two positive rational weights with a common positive natural denominator, repeat each base according to its positive numerator, and apply the strict equality clause of [[thm-am-gm]] to this finite list. If the bases differ the list is not constant and the inequality is strict; clearing the root preserves strictness. The existing proof of the weighted supplier supplies this finite-repetition construction; rational representations and embeddings are recorded in [[lem-rat-positive-denominator]], [[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-of-q-embeds]] and the rational power laws. In the three cases above the bases differ whenever $y\ne1$ (for negative $r$, equality $y=y^r$ would give $y^{1-r}=1$, contradicting positive-exponent monotonicity). Therefore the asserted equality conditions follow without inventing an equality clause in the supplier. Finally for $r\ge2$ put $s=r/2\ge1$ and $z=y^2>0$, and apply the just-proved rational Bernoulli bound to $z$: $y^r=z^s\ge1+s(z-1)=1+rx+(r/2)x^2$. This uses $z-1>-1$ even when $-1<x<0$, so the full stated $x$ domain is valid. Equality is $s=1$ or $z=1$; because $y>0$, the latter is $y=1$. Replacing $r/2$ by a natural $m\le r/2$ only decreases the nonnegative quadratic term. The floor notation is explanatory, not an invocation of a later floor supplier.

Rational endpoint $x=-1$: the supplementary clause of [[def-rational-power]] sets $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$. Thus for $r\ge1$ the lower inequality is $0\ge1-r$, with equality exactly at $r=1$, and for $0<r\le1$ the reversed inequality is $0\le1-r$, again with equality exactly at $r=1$. At $r=0$ use the existing integer-power convention $0^0=1$, yielding equality. Negative $r$ are excluded here because zero has no inverse. For $r\ge2$ the quadratic bound reduces to $0\ge1-r/2$, equal exactly at $r=2$. This handles the endpoint directly; it does not apply the positive-base weighted theorem at a zero base or silently extend its hypotheses.

references.title: Jim Belk, Convexity, Inequalities, and Norms (Cornell University)
references.locator: Theorem 5, pp. 5-6, weighted AM-GM statement and convexity/exponential proof. Only the statement is corroborating context here: the published rational-weight supplier supplies a complete finite proof, and the Bernoulli consequences below are derived locally. No exponential/convexity theorem is consumed.

items.title: Five finite AM-GM proofs, with the same sharp equality case
items.statement: For a natural $n\ge1$ and nonnegative reals $a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}$, put $A=(\sum_{k<n}a_k)/n$ and $G=(\prod_{k<n}a_k)^{1/n}$, using the unique nonnegative root. Five finite routes verify $\prod_{k<n}a_k\le A^n$, equivalently $G\le A$, with equality exactly when every entry is the same. They are Cauchy's forward-backward induction, ordinary induction by sum-preserving replacement, ordinary induction by product-preserving replacement, ordinary induction from the independently proved integer Bernoulli inequality, and binary averaging with geometric-mean padding. The last route stops after one padding argument, rather than the backward descent used by the first. No route invokes a derivative, logarithm, exponential, convergence or an unproved optimization theorem.
items.strategy:
Use [[def-finite-sum]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] for sums and products in $\mathbb R$, and embed natural lengths before field operations. By [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] and [[lem-power-monotone]], proving $\prod a_k\le A^n$ is equivalent to $G\le A$ because $A,G\ge0$. Handle $n=1$ first. If some entry is zero, the product and $G$ are zero, so the inequality is immediate; equality is $A=0$, which by nonnegativity of the summands means every entry is zero. Hence every nontrivial proof route may assume all entries positive, so $A,G>0$ and every division below is legal.

Route 1, Cauchy forward-backward induction: use the existing full proof and equality clause of [[thm-am-gm]], not a duplicate supplier. Its two-entry base is $((u+v)/2)^2-uv=(u-v)^2/4\ge0$, strict when $u\ne v$. Write the doubling lengths as natural numbers $N_0=1$, $N_{j+1}=N_j+N_j$ via [[thm-recursion]]; do not use real-field powers as list lengths. The two-entry bound combines two equal-sized blocks, so $P(N)$ implies $P(N+N)$ with equality only when each half is constant and both half-means agree. The backward step $P(m+1)\Rightarrow P(m)$ appends the $m$-entry arithmetic mean $A$; the augmented mean is still $A$, and cancellation of the positive $A$ from $P_m A\le A^{m+1}$ gives $P_m\le A^m$. Induction gives $N_j\ge j+1$, so $N_n>n$; descent from $N_n$ to $n$ is a finite natural induction on the missing length, exactly as in the published supplier. Appended means do not change whether the original entries are all equal.

Route 2, sum-preserving finite replacement: prove by ordinary induction on $n$ that any positive $n$ entries of sum $n$ have product at most $1$, with equality only for the constant list $1$. The $n=1$ case is immediate. For a nonconstant normalized list, there are entries $u<1<v$: otherwise a list entirely on one side of $1$, with a strict entry, would have sum strictly below or above $n$. Replace these two entries by $1,w$ with $w=u+v-1>0$. The sum stays fixed and the product of the pair strictly increases, since $w-uv=(1-u)(v-1)>0$. Remove the newly fixed $1$; the remaining $n-1$ positive entries have sum $n-1$, so by the induction hypothesis their product is at most $1$. The original product is strictly smaller than the replacement product, hence $<1$. The constant list gives equality. Apply this result to $a_k/A$, whose sum is $n$, and multiply by $A^n$. The replacement is a proof step on a finite list, not an infinite smoothing process or an invocation of existence of a maximum.

Route 3, product-preserving finite replacement: prove by ordinary induction on $n$ that positive $n$ entries of product $1$ have sum at least $n$, with equality only for the constant list $1$. Again the base is immediate. In a nonconstant product-one list there must be $u<1<v$; products of entries all on one side of $1$ are strictly on that side unless they all equal $1$. Replace $u,v$ by $1,uv$, preserving the product while strictly decreasing the sum because $u+v-1-uv=(1-u)(v-1)>0$. Remove the $1$ and apply the $(n-1)$-entry induction hypothesis, proving the original sum is strictly greater than $n$. For the given list, divide every entry by $G$: the product is $1$ since $G^n=\prod a_k$, so $\sum a_k/G\ge n$, giving $A\ge G$, with the stated strict/equality alternatives. This finite induction differs from Route 2 by fixing the product and decreasing the sum.

Route 4, integer Bernoulli induction: this route uses only [[lem-bernoulli-inequality]], whose actual published proof is ordinary induction from order arithmetic; it does not use the AM-GM-derived rational extension in the other new example. Suppose the AM-GM claim and equality clause hold at length $n-1$ with $n\ge2$. Let $B=(\sum_{k<n-1}a_k)/(n-1)>0$, $c=a_{n-1}>0$, $t=c/B>0$, and $h=(t-1)/n>-1$. The induction hypothesis gives $\prod_{k<n}a_k\le B^{n-1}c=B^n t$. The full integer Bernoulli bound at $h,n$ gives $(A/B)^n=(1+h)^n\ge1+nh=t$, so $\prod a_k\le A^n$. Equality forces equality both in the $(n-1)$-entry hypothesis and in Bernoulli. Since $n\ge2$, Bernoulli equality implies $h=0$, thus $c=B$; the former equality makes all remaining entries equal to $B$. Conversely a constant list gives equality. This proves the ordinary inductive step from $1$ to every natural length without circular use of AM-GM in the Bernoulli supplier.

Route 5, binary averaging and geometric-mean padding: derive $P(N_j)$ directly from the square identity in Route 1 by induction on the doubling natural lengths $N_j$, with the full equality clause. In the step split a positive list of length $N+N$ into two length-$N$ halves with means $U,V$. The induction hypothesis bounds the product by $U^N V^N=(UV)^N$, and $UV\le((U+V)/2)^2$ bounds this by the $N+N$ power of the whole mean. Equality implies both halves are constant and $U=V$, hence the whole list is constant. Now choose $N=N_n\ge n$ and append $N-n$ copies of the *geometric* mean $G$ of the original list. The padded product is $G^n G^{N-n}=G^N$. The binary-length inequality gives $G\le(\sum_{k<n}a_k+(N-n)G)/N$, so subtracting $(N-n)G$ yields $nG\le\sum a_k$. Equality in the final inequality is exactly equality for the padded list, so all original entries equal $G$; this remains true if no entries needed appending. There is no backward descent: this uses one finite padding by $G$, in contrast with Route 1's arithmetic-mean descent. The natural length difference and all shifted finite sums are justified by natural-order/discrete arithmetic and the finite-sum laws.
